title: Cold-swap evacuate, queue-drain and capacity-priming notes (WIP)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working runbook for low-frequency, higher-impact hardware maintenance we call 'cold-swap'—physical GPU/node replacement that requires the host to be powered down and reimaged. Goal is to minimize service impact by coordinating a safe evacuation (queue-drain), priming capacity elsewhere, and verifying post-swap health before putting node back into rotation.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to on-prem racks and colocation hosts where hot-swap is not possible (cartridge/firmware restrictions).
- Targets inference node pools that host GPU-backed pods (inference and KV cache sidecars).
- Assumes SRE oncall and platform-owner coordination; not for ad-hoc uncoordinated work.
- We distinguish 'cold-swap' from 'hot-swap' steps (hot-swap doc exists separately).

Preflight checklist (must pass before powering down):
- Announce maintenance: Slack #sre with ETA and scope, tag @oncall and impacted product owners.
- Check active request rate: grafana/dashboard -> inference.token_rate (last 15m) should be below threshold for planned window. If bursty, postpone.
- Capacity priming: ensure warm pool nodes available or spin up on cloud dedicated pool. Target: +20% available GPU capacity in affected AZ before drain.
- Verify model cache persistence policy: whether models are ephemeral (will need to reprovision) or persistent on node local nvme. Document model artifacts to warm after swap.
- Identify pods pinned to node: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide | grep <node>. Copy list to incident notes.
- Lock CI/CD deploys for the cluster (prevent rollouts during operation).

Evacuation / queue-drain procedure (step-by-step):
1) Cordon the node (prevent new scheduling):
   kubectl cordon <node-name>
   Confirm: kubectl get nodes | grep <node-name> (Should show 'SchedulingDisabled')

2) Signal inference queue manager to stop sending new requests to node-specific routing buckets (if using smart-routing):
   - For smart-router, tag node with taint: kubectl taint nodes <node-name> node-maintenance=drain:NoSchedule
   - Patch routing config: POST /router/admin/disable-backend/<node-id> (internal endpoint)
   Confirm router logs show drain ack.

3) Begin graceful drain for pods with a timeout. Prefer eviction over delete where possible:
   kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=15m
   Notes: set --grace-period to at least 120s to allow in-flight inference to complete and commit KV caches if configured to flush on SIGTERM.

4) Monitor pod termination and queue depth:
   - kubectl get pods --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name>
   - Watch: inference.pending_requests gauge, router.queue_depth metrics; ensure pending_requests approaches zero for node-specific queues before step 5.

5) Force-migrate any stubborn pods after safety window: kubectl delete pod <pod> --namespace <ns> --grace-period=30 (only after confirming no critical in-flight state).

6) Confirm node free of production pods (daemonsets like node-exporter will remain): kubectl get pods --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name> --all-namespaces

Powerdown and hardware swap notes:
- Only authorized SRE or datacenter tech should power cycle. Record power actions in the incident chat.
- Record serial numbers of removed GPU(s), firmware versions, and any visible physical faults (photos ok).
- Re-image or apply approved image bundle (image id recorded in infra repo). Include nvidia driver version that matches driver ABI for runtime (e.g., 535.xx).
- After reimage, confirm kernel modules: nvidia-smi, nvidia-container-runtime status, NVMe mount points for model cache.

Post-swap bring-up and capacity priming:
1) Verify node is healthy at kube-level: kubelet registers and node status Ready. kubectl get nodes | grep <node-name>
2) Remove maintenance taint: kubectl taint nodes <node-name> node-maintenance:NoSchedule-
3) Put node into probationed pool initially: add label 'probation=true' so scheduler keeps lower priority for new pods.
4) Warm caches and models before accepting production load: run pre-warm job to pull models into local cache and run 2-3 short inference queries per model to populate KV cache. Script: /opt/scripts/warm-models.sh <node-name> --models modelA,modelB
   - Verify local model checksum and model-serving readiness endpoint: curl http://<node-ip>:9100/ready | grep ready
5) Gradually re-enable routing buckets or remove probation label after monitoring: remove 'probation=true' after 10m of stable metrics.

Observability and validation gates (required before fully re-enabling):
- Token latency p50/p95 for this node's subset should be within baseline ±10% for 10m.
- No elevated 5xx from inference containers.
- GPU utilization should ramp predictably during priming (no immediate OOMs or driver errors).
- Router queues should not exceed threshold (router.queue_depth < 5 per backend).
- No increased pod restarts/crashloops in last 10m.

Rollback / abort conditions (immediately stop and escalate):
- Node fails to register with kubelet after 10m -> escalate to hardware team and revert by removing from pool and reassigning workloads to spare nodes.
- Driver errors on nvidia-smi or container runtime failures -> rollback image or escalate to infra-devs; do not re-enable routing.
- Persistent model load failures or disk corruption -> mark node as quarantined and schedule deeper forensic work.

Temporary capacity injection strategy (if priming pool not sufficient):
- Fast path: spin ephemeral cloud GPUs (if allowed) and route a percentage of traffic via cross-region policy for degraded latency tolerant customers.
- Medium path: increase batch size and prefetch on surviving nodes to reduce per-token compute until capacity recovered. Monitor quality regression.

Open items / TODOs (WIP):
- Automate warm-models.sh per-node parallelization and add a retry/backoff when a model server returns 503s.
- Add a router API that accepts a probation label and automatically shifts % of traffic over a 10m ramp.
- Document precise KV cache flush semantics on SIGTERM for all inference images (missing for modelX at time of writing).
- Decide a consistent grace-period default per model class (small vs large LLMS).

Post-incident data capture checklist (collect after operation):
- Grafana snapshot (15m before / during / 30m after): token_rate, token_lat_p50/p95, router.queue_depth, pod_restarts, node_gpu_errors, node_disk_errors.
- kubectl describe node <node-name> and save output.
- dmesg and journalctl from time around failure (if hardware fault).
- Photos and serial numbers of replaced hardware.
- Record all Slack timestamps and operators involved for postmortem.

Communication template (short):
- Pre-maintenance: "SRE maintenance scheduled for <node-name> in <rack/az> at <time>. Expected downtime for node only, service impact: none if priming successful. Contact: @Maya."
- Mid-maintenance: "Node <node-name> cordoned and drained. Performing GPU swap. Monitoring priming pool performance."
- Post-maintenance: "Node <node-name> brought back, warmed, and removed from probation at <time>. All metrics nominal. Follow-up: postmortem in Confluence link."

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep the drain window under 20 minutes for low-latency customers; if longer, consider partial shift of low-priority traffic out.
- Double-check driver-ABI matrix before reimage (we burned a node last quarter with a mismatched toolkit).
- Consider adding a node labelling convention 'warm-level=auto' to trigger automatic warm jobs when node becomes Ready.

References and quick links:
- internal router admin endpoints: https://router-admin.internal/
- infra image bundles: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/images
- SRE rota: confluence.redwood/sre/rota

Contact escalation:
- Primary SRE oncall: @oncall (pager)
- Infra platform lead: Ethan Park (ethan@redwood.example.com)
- Hardware vendor ops: hw-ops@colocation.example.com

End of draft. Will iterate with Claire and Jamal to add automation stubs and a straight-to-run sequence for emergency windows.
